name: The Structure of the Sky — elements, modalities, signs, houses and aspects
description: The skeleton the voices hang on, as plain data: not a voice, not an interpretation. Leaves: the four elements, three modalities, two polarities, ten planets (seven classical; Uranus, Neptune and Pluto marked modern), twelve houses and the aspects. Emergences, by composite_of: every sign is its element + modality + polarity; the triplicities and the modality groups are their signs; the houses group as angular / succedent / cadent, as six axes, four quadrants and four halves. Relations that are not 'made of' — rulers, exaltation, detriment, fall, triplicity rulers, opposites — sit in metadata. Each item's 'Traditions' section says which traditions use it, cited to a public-domain text already in this repo (Ptolemy tr. Ashmand 1822, Lilly 1647, Alan Leo, the Bṛhat Jātaka tr. Iyer 1885) or to research/bibliography.bib; where no citation was found, the claim was left out. ASPECTS ARE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN PLACEMENTS: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored — the aspect items here define the relationship, they do not belong to any chart. CROSS-LINKS: every sign, planet, house and aspect item in the voice grammars carries metadata.source_deck = 'the-structure-of-the-sky', metadata.source_item_id = the id here, metadata.deck = 'The Structure of the Sky' — the one cross-link pattern, which the cards viewer renders as an 'Open in …' pill. How an AI reads with this grammar: CLAUDE-AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md. Under the creed: a chart is a mirror and a calendar, never a command — structure describes where things stand; it predicts nothing.

sections.Structure: Twelve signs of 30° each around the ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path. Each sign is one element, one modality and one polarity; the four triplicities hold all twelve, and so do the three modality groups — two ways of cutting the same circle.
sections.Traditions:
- Tropical: Ptolemy takes 'the sign of Aries, which commences at the vernal equinox' as the beginning of the circle, so the signs follow the seasons — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 12. Ashmand's note 42 adds that the stars have moved while the signs have not.
- Jyotiṣa counts its rāśis in a **sidereal** zodiac, measured from the fixed stars, where Ptolemy's zodiac begins at the vernal equinox; the two circles now sit roughly 24° apart, so a sidereal sign of the same name is not the same stretch of sky (research/views/jyotisa.md [@pingree1997; @campion2008]; grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka description).

sections.Structure: Fire is one of the four elements. Three signs carry it — Aries, Leo, Sagittarius — each four signs (120°) from the next, so the three draw an equilateral triangle on the circle: that triangle is the fire triplicity (see the item 'Fire triplicity'). All three fire signs are masculine. Signs of one element meet by trine; fire and air signs meet by sextile and opposition.
sections.Traditions:
- Lilly names this triangle the 'Fiery Triplicity', and gives its signs the qualities hot and dry — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647]; wording as quoted sign by sign in grammars/william-lilly-christian-astrology.
- Alan Leo uses the same element names for the triplicities — Alan Leo, *Astrology for All* (1899), as quoted in grammars/alan-leo.
- Ptolemy groups the same three signs as his first triplicity, but names it by number, by sex and by wind, not by element — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 21.

sections.Structure: The cardinal signs are the four whose first degree the Sun reaches at an equinox or a solstice — Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn — so each opens a season. The four are each three signs (90°) apart, so they form a square on the circle: every sign of one modality meets the others by square or by opposition, one of each element.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy splits this group in two: Cancer and Capricorn are *tropical* (the Sun 'seems to turn' there, at the solstices), Aries and Libra *equinoctial* (day and night equal) — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 14.
- Lilly: 'moveable' and 'cardinal', because the Sun's entry into them opens the quarters of the year — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647], the chapter on the division of the signs.
- Bṛhat Jātaka: 'Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn are movable signs' (cara) — Varāhamihira, *Bṛhat Jātaka*, tr. N. Chidambaram Iyer (1885), as quoted in grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka, ch. I st. 11.
- Alan Leo calls the three groups cardinal, fixed and mutable — Alan Leo, *Astrology for All* (1899), as quoted in grammars/alan-leo.

sections.Structure: The fixed signs are the four that follow the cardinal ones — Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius — the middle month of each season. The four are each three signs (90°) apart, so they form a square on the circle: every sign of one modality meets the others by square or by opposition, one of each element.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: *fixed*, because while the Sun is in them the season begun in the sign before 'is then more firmly established' — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 14.
- Lilly: 'fixed', the season being then fixed and plainly felt — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647].
- Bṛhat Jātaka: 'Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius are fixed signs' (sthira) — Varāhamihira, *Bṛhat Jātaka*, tr. N. Chidambaram Iyer (1885), as quoted in grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka, ch. I st. 11.
- Alan Leo calls the three groups cardinal, fixed and mutable — Alan Leo, *Astrology for All* (1899), as quoted in grammars/alan-leo.

sections.Structure: The mutable signs are the four that close each season — Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces — lying between a fixed sign and the next cardinal one. The four are each three signs (90°) apart, so they form a square on the circle: every sign of one modality meets the others by square or by opposition, one of each element.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: *bicorporeal*, placed between the fixed and the tropical signs and sharing the properties of both — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 14.
- Lilly: 'common', also 'by-corporal or double-bodied' — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647].
- Bṛhat Jātaka: 'common signs' (dvisvabhāva), said to be 'both movable and fixed' — Varāhamihira, *Bṛhat Jātaka*, tr. N. Chidambaram Iyer (1885), as quoted in grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka, ch. I st. 11.
- Alan Leo calls the three groups cardinal, fixed and mutable — Alan Leo, *Astrology for All* (1899), as quoted in grammars/alan-leo.

sections.Structure: The twelve signs alternate, one masculine, one feminine, starting with Aries as masculine. The masculine signs are the odd-numbered ones — Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius — which are the fire and air signs. The traditional words are kept here as the sources' own terms.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: 'six are called masculine and diurnal, and six feminine and nocturnal', 'arranged in alternate order … as the day is followed by the night'. He also reports a minority practice that starts the count from the rising sign instead of from Aries — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 15.
- Lilly keeps the pairing: masculine and diurnal signs — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647]; see the sign chapters quoted in grammars/william-lilly-christian-astrology.
- Bṛhat Jātaka: 'the odd signs are all malefic and masculine', the even signs 'benefic and feminine' — Varāhamihira, *Bṛhat Jātaka*, tr. N. Chidambaram Iyer (1885), as quoted in grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka, ch. I st. 11.

sections.Structure: The twelve signs alternate, one feminine, one masculine, starting with Aries as masculine. The feminine signs are the even-numbered ones — Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, Pisces — which are the earth and water signs. The traditional words are kept here as the sources' own terms.

sections.Structure: Aries is the 1st sign: **fire** + **cardinal** + **masculine** — the only sign with that element and that modality. It shares its element with Leo and Sagittarius (trine), its modality with Cancer and Capricorn (square) and Libra (opposition). Libra, its opposite, has the same modality and polarity and the paired element (air).

Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn — the bodies visible without a telescope, and the only planets in Ptolemy, Lilly and the Bṛhat Jātaka. Every sign has one of them as its classical ruler: the Sun and Moon one sign each, the other five two each.

Uranus (1781), Neptune (1846), Pluto (1930): found with telescopes, so absent from every text before them. Modern astrology uses them; the historical voices in this library do not, except Alan Leo for the first two.

Sun is one of the seven classical planets — the bodies visible to the naked eye that every historical voice in this library counts. It rules Leo; it is exalted in Aries; it is in detriment in Aquarius (the sign opposite its own) and in fall in Libra (the sign opposite its exaltation). Where Sun stands in a chart is a placement: a sign, a house, and the aspects it makes to the other placements. Those three things are read from the rest of this grammar.

sections.Structure: Uranus was found with a telescope in 1781, so it is absent from every text written before then. It is marked **modern**: it belongs to astrology after its discovery only. Modern practice gives it Aquarius as a sign to rule, beside that sign's classical ruler, Saturn; the traditional dignity table has no place for it.
sections.Traditions:
- Not among Ptolemy's or Lilly's planets: both count seven — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822]; William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647].
- Alan Leo's *Astrology for All* describes it astronomically ('commonly called Herschel after its re-discoverer') [@web_leo_astrologyforall], and his *How to Judge a Nativity* (quoted from the archive.org scan of the 1928 printing) says 'Uranus has a natural sympathy with Scorpio' [@web_leo_howtojudge] — an early modern view that differs from the later Aquarius convention.
- Not a graha of the Bṛhat Jātaka, which counts nine: the seven planets and the two lunar nodes — grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka.
- The modern rulership (Uranus–Aquarius) is carried here as it is carried in grammars/dignities-rulerships (`modern_co_ruler`), where it is marked a modern addition; no public-domain source in this repo states it as settled.

sections.Structure: Twelve places counted from the rising point of the eastern horizon. They are fixed to the horizon and meridian of one time and place, where the signs are fixed to the sky: the same planet has a sign from the date, a house from the date, the hour and the place.
sections.Traditions:
- Whole-sign houses: Brennan argues that Hellenistic astrologers counted each whole sign as one house, starting from the rising sign, and the method has been revived since the 1990s (research/views/contemporary-resurgence.md [@brennan2017]). Confidence: medium — one scholar-practitioner's reconstruction.
- Quadrant houses: Lilly divides the sky 'into four equal arcs by the Meridian and Horizon', and each quadrant into three, beginning from the East — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647] (OCR scan). This repo's chart viewer computes its own house cusps; how is out of scope here.

sections.Structure: The 1st house is angular — one of the four angles, where the horizon and the meridian cross the circle. It sits below the horizon, in the eastern half of the chart, in Lilly's fourth quadrant. Its opposite is the 7th house: together they make the 1–7 axis. A house is a place in the turning sky at one moment and place on earth; which sign falls on it depends on that moment.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy treats the four angles as the cardinal points of the horizon: this is 'the eastern point, or angle of the ascendant', which he calls chiefly dry in nature — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 13.
- Lilly counts the houses from the East, dividing each quadrant made by the meridian and the horizon into three, and ranks them: angles 'most powerful', succedents next, cadents 'of little efficacy'; this house is angular — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647], the chapter on the division of the heavens (read from the archive.org OCR scan; wording paraphrased).

sections.Structure: The half of the chart above the horizon: Lilly's first and second quadrants. A planet's hemisphere is a fact of the moment: it follows from the time and place, as the houses do.
The half of the chart below the horizon: Lilly's third and fourth quadrants. A planet's hemisphere is a fact of the moment: it follows from the time and place, as the houses do.

The half of the chart east of the meridian, around the ascendant: Lilly's first and fourth quadrants. A planet's hemisphere is a fact of the moment: it follows from the time and place, as the houses do.

The half of the chart west of the meridian, around the descendant: Lilly's second and third quadrants. A planet's hemisphere is a fact of the moment: it follows from the time and place, as the houses do.

Two placements in the same sign (0°). Sign-by-sign they share everything: element, modality, polarity. Strictly it is not a configuration between two parts of the zodiac but one part. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy's chapter on configurations leaves the conjunction out; Ashmand's note explains that it treats only parts configured *with each other*, while he uses the conjunction elsewhere — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 16 and note 44.
- Lilly: 'we use to call the Conjunction an Aspect, but very improperly' — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647] (read from the archive.org OCR scan; spelling modernised).

sections.Structure: Two signs apart (60°, a sixth of the circle). The signs share polarity but not element or modality: a sextile always joins fire with air, or earth with water. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: the hexagonal distance, 'two signs, or sixty degrees'; with the trine it is 'harmonious, because they are constituted between signs of the same kind; being formed between either all feminine or all masculine signs' — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 16.
- Lilly: 'the sixth part of the Zodiack' — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647].

sections.Structure: Three signs apart (90°, a quarter). The signs share modality — both cardinal, both fixed or both mutable — but not polarity, and never element. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: the quadrate distance, 'three signs, or ninety degrees'; with the opposition 'considered to be discordant, because they are configurations made between signs not of the same kind, but of different natures and sexes' — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 16.
- Lilly: the 'Quadrate' or 'Tetragonall' aspect, 'a fourth part of the Circle' — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647].

sections.Structure: Four signs apart (120°, a third). The signs share element — they are two corners of one triplicity — and therefore polarity, but not modality. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: the triangular distance, 'four signs, or a hundred and twenty degrees'; harmonious, between signs of the same kind — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 16. His triplicities (ch. 21) are the same triangles.
- Lilly: 'a third part of the Circle', also called 'Trigonall'; 'three Signs make one Trygon or Triplicity' — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647] (OCR scan; spelling modernised).
- Alan Leo: 'the trine, 120°, is a third of the circle' — *How to Judge a Nativity*, as quoted in grammars/alan-leo.

sections.Structure: Six signs apart (180°, half). Opposite signs share modality and polarity; their elements differ but pair across the circle the way a sextile pairs them: fire with air, earth with water. Each sign has exactly one opposite. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: the diametrical distance, 'six signs, or a hundred and eighty degrees'; discordant, with the square — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 16. Read against his own ch. 15, opposite signs are of the same sex (Aries and Libra are both 'masculine and diurnal'), so the sex difference he names fits the square, not the opposition. The tension is in the text as translated and is left standing here.
- Lilly: 'Opposition or Diametral Radiation', planets '180 degrees, or half the Circle' apart — William Lilly, *Christian Astrology* (1647) [@lilly1647]. He also pairs the signs and the houses as opposites for erecting a figure: 'the tenth house is opposite to the fourth'.

sections.Structure: Five signs apart (150°). The two signs share nothing — not element, not modality, not polarity. Not one of the classical (Ptolemaic) aspects. An aspect is a relationship between two placements, not a thing a chart owns: a chart's aspects are computed from where its planets stand, never stored.
sections.Traditions:
- Ptolemy: signs five apart (and signs one apart) are *inconjunct* — 'they divide the whole circle into unequal parts' and share in none of the four configurations — Ptolemy, *Tetrabiblos*, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) [@ptolemyashmand1822], Book I ch. 19. Ashmand's note records that later aspects (semiquadrate, quintile, sesquiquadrate, biquintile) were added after Ptolemy.
